tips.title: Spanish drops "I" and "you"
tips.body: In Spanish, the verb's ending already tells you who is doing it. Soy means I am and eres means you are, so you don't need a separate word for I or you. To say I'm from Chile, just say soy de Chile. Add yo (I) or tú (you) only when you want to stress the person or compare two people, as in English when you say I am, but you are.

examples.target: Yo soy Luis y tú eres Ana.

tips.title: Two verbs for "to be"
tips.body: Spanish has two verbs that both mean to be: ser and estar. Use ser (soy, eres, es) for what someone is: their name, where they're from, their job, what they're like. Use estar (estoy, estás, está) for how someone is right now and where they are. So soy de México tells people where you come from, but estoy bien tells them how you feel today. If it's about how you feel or where you are at the moment, reach for estar.

examples.target: Soy Ana y estoy muy bien.
examples.en: I'm Ana and I'm very well.

examples.target: Él es de Chile y está aquí.
examples.en: He's from Chile and he's here.

tips.title: Verbs change with who does them
tips.body: A Spanish verb changes its ending to show who is doing it. Quiero means I want, quieres means you want, and quiere means he or she wants. Tener works the same way: tengo is I have, tienes is you have, and tiene is he or she has. Most of the time, an ending in -o means I, an ending in -s means you, and an ending in -e means he or she. Listen for the ending, because it tells you who, even when nobody says yo, tú or ella.

examples.target: Ella quiere un café y tiene mi café.
examples.en: She wants a coffee and has my coffee.

tips.title: Every noun is el or la
tips.body: In Spanish, every noun (a word for a person or a thing) is either masculine or feminine. Masculine words use el for the and un for a, like el hermano and un amigo. Feminine words use la for the and una for a, like la hermana and una amiga. This is true for things too, so coffee is masculine: el café. Words ending in -o are usually el and words ending in -a are usually la, but not always, so learn el or la together with each new word.

examples.target: Tengo un hermano y una hermana.
examples.en: I have a brother and a sister.

examples.target: La madre de Ana está aquí.

tips.title: Describing words come after and match
tips.body: In Spanish, a describing word usually comes after the thing it describes, so a big coffee is un café grande. It also matches that thing: use the -o ending for an el word and the -a ending for a la word, as in un amigo nuevo and una amiga nueva. When there is more than one, add -s to both words, as in dos amigos nuevos. Words that end in -e, like grande, are the same for el words and la words. So say the thing first, then make the describing word's ending match it.

examples.target: Mi hermana tiene una amiga nueva.
examples.en: My sister has a new friend.

tips.title: Questions and ¿ ¡
tips.body: In Spanish, a question opens with an upside-down ¿ and closes with ?, so you know from the start that it's a question. Exclamations work the same way, with ¡ at the start and ! at the end, as in ¡Hola! For a yes-or-no question, you can take a normal sentence and raise your voice at the end: eres de México means you are from Mexico, and ¿Eres de México? asks it. Question words always carry an accent mark, like qué, dónde and cómo. The accent doesn't change the sound much, but it marks the word as a question word, so keep it when you ask.

tips.title: No goes before the verb
tips.body: To say not in Spanish, you just put no right before the action word, the verb. So sé means I know, and no sé means I don't know. Spanish has no extra word like don't, so no entiendo means I don't understand. When you answer a question with no, you often say it twice: No, no sé means No, I don't know. The first no answers the question, and the second no goes before the verb.

tips.title: Tú and usted
tips.body: Spanish has two ways to say you. Use tú with friends, family and people your age, and usted to be polite with strangers and older people. With usted, the verb takes the same form as for he or she, so you say puede, not puedes. ¿Puedes ayudarme? asks a friend for help, and ¿Puede ayudarme? asks a stranger politely. If you're not sure which one to use, usted is the safe choice.

examples.en: Excuse me, can you help me?

tips.title: Going to: voy a…
tips.body: To talk about plans, Spanish uses ir a, just like going to in English. Take the right form of ir (voy, vas or va), add a, then add a second verb. That second verb stays in its basic form, the one ending in -ar, -er or -ir that you'd find in a dictionary, like hablar or entender. So voy a hablar means I'm going to speak, and ¿vas a venir? means are you going to come? Add hoy or mañana to say when your plan happens.

examples.en: Are you going to be home today?

examples.target: Mi amiga va a necesitar ayuda mañana.
examples.en: My friend is going to need help tomorrow.

tips.title: Regular -ar, -er and -ir verbs
tips.body: Most Spanish verbs follow one of three patterns, depending on whether they end in -ar, -er or -ir. To use one, drop that ending and add a new one that shows who is doing it. For I, add -o: hablo means I speak, como means I eat, vivo means I live. For you, add -as to -ar verbs and -es to the others: hablas, comes, vives. For he or she, add -a to -ar verbs and -e to the others: habla, come, vive.

tips.title: Gustar works backwards
tips.body: Spanish says I like backwards: me gusta el café really means the coffee pleases me. The thing you like does the pleasing, so the verb matches that thing, not you. Say me gusta for one thing and me gustan for two or more things. To ask someone if they like something, swap me for te: ¿te gusta el café? means do you like coffee?

tips.title: Me, te, lo go before the verb
tips.body: The small words for me, you, him, her and it are me, te, lo and la, and they go right before the verb. So I love you is te quiero, which word for word is you I love. Lo veo means I see him or I see it, and la veo means I see her. When the verb is in its dictionary form, the one ending in -ar, -er or -ir, the small word attaches to the end of it instead. So to help me is ayudarme, all one word.

examples.en: I love you so much, my love.

tips.title: Por and para
tips.body: Por and para can both mean for, but they point in different directions. Para looks ahead to a goal or to the person who gets something: para mi madre means for my mother, and para comer means in order to eat. Para can also give a deadline, so para mañana means by tomorrow. Por looks back at a reason or an exchange: you already know por favor, and gracias por todo means thanks for everything. Por can also mean through or around a place, so por aquí means around here.

examples.target: Este café es para mi madre.
examples.en: This coffee is for my mother.
Is there a bathroom around here?

tips.title: Talking about the past
tips.body: To talk about something that already happened, Spanish changes the end of the verb. For -ar verbs like hablar, drop the -ar and add -é for I or -ó for he or she, so hablé means I spoke and habló means he or she spoke. Say the accent clearly, because hablo with no accent means I speak, right now. Some very common verbs have their own short past forms, so learn them as words: tuve means I had, and hice means I did or I made. Fue has two meanings: it was, and he or she went, and the rest of the sentence tells you which one.

examples.en: I talked to Ana and she talked to me.

examples.en: My father went to the party.

example.en: I'm calling you from the car.

cards.trick: DESDE sounds like "the stage": you watch the whole show from the stage.
cards.why: Use desde for the point something starts from or is seen from; de for where someone or something comes from.

example.en: Are you guys coming to the party?

cards.trick: USTEDES sounds like "use the days": you all use the days together.
cards.why: Use ustedes for two or more people; usted or tú is for one.

example.en: There's no reason to cry.

cards.trick: RAZÓN sounds like a Spanish-accented REASON (rah-SOHN), and that is just what it means.

example.en: I listen to music while I work.

cards.trick: MIENTRAS sounds like 'me in trance': I stay in a trance while the music plays.

example.en: Are you being serious?

cards.trick: SERIO sounds like serious without the ending: a serious face never finishes its smile.

cards.hint: short filler that opens a reply, not bueno

example.target: Pues no sé, tal vez mañana.
example.en: Well, I don't know, maybe tomorrow.

cards.trick: PUES sounds like pause: you say it when you pause before answering, like well.
cards.why: Use pues to pause before a reply; use bueno to mean okay or to accept something.

example.en: I don't have health insurance.

cards.trick: SEGURO sounds like "secure": insurance keeps your money secure when things go wrong.

example.target: Mi equipo ganó el partido anoche.
example.en: My team won the game last night.

cards.trick: GANAR sounds like gonna: you're gonna win, so raise the trophy!

example.en: I work under a lot of pressure.

cards.trick: BAJO sounds like 'bah, ho-hum': you mutter it when you're stuck under pressure.

cards.hint: same word as less, not excepto

example.en: Everyone came except your brother.

cards.trick: MENOS sounds like "minus": everyone minus me means everyone except me.

example.en: I still haven't eaten anything.

cards.trick: AÚN sounds like a-MOON: the moon is still up in the sky, and it isn't morning yet.

example.target: ¡Qué buena idea! Vamos a la playa.
example.en: What a good idea! Let's go to the beach.

cards.trick: IDEA is spelled just like English idea; say it ee-DAY-ah, as if a new idea lights up your day.

example.en: I have nothing against you.

cards.trick: CONTRA sounds like contrary: being contrary means going against everything.

example.target: Es la segunda vez que llamas hoy.
example.en: It's the second time you've called today.

cards.trick: SEGUNDO sounds like "second-oh": oh, you came second again!

example.en: It rained a lot during the night.

cards.trick: DURANTE sounds like "during" plus "ante": things that happen during something endure through it.

example.en: You arrived late again.

cards.trick: TARDE sounds like "tardy": a tardy student always shows up late.

cards.hint: not nadie; none out of a group

example.en: None of my friends came.

cards.trick: NINGUNO sounds like "nin-GONE-o": every one of them is gone, so none are left.
cards.why: Use ninguno for none out of a known group; nadie for nobody at all.

example.en: We walked toward the beach.

cards.trick: HACIA sounds like "ah, see ya": you wave and head toward your friend across the street.

example.target: Te amo con todo mi corazón.
example.en: I love you with all my heart.

cards.trick: AMAR sounds like amour, the French word for love, as in a grand romance.
cards.why: Use amar for deep, intense love, like a partner; use querer for everyday love for family and friends.

cards.hint: of a color, as in light blue

example.en: I want a light blue shirt.

cards.trick: CLARO is a clear, bright shade: azul claro is light blue, close to clear.

example.en: There are too many people here.

cards.trick: DEMASIADO sounds like "the massive dose": a massive dose is always too much.

cards.hint: in negatives, often after ni; not incluso

example.en: He didn't even call me yesterday.

cards.trick: SIQUIERA sounds like 'see, key? Era...': you can't even see the key you lost.
cards.why: Use siquiera for even in negatives (ni siquiera); use incluso or hasta for even in positive sentences.

example.target: Siempre olvido mis llaves en casa.
example.en: I always forget my keys at home.

cards.trick: OLVIDAR sounds like "all video": you watched so many videos that you forgot everything else.

example.target: Voy a ir aunque estoy cansado.
example.en: I'm going to go even though I'm tired.

cards.trick: AUNQUE sounds like "own key": although you own a key, you still knock on the door.

example.target: Por fin conseguí dormir un poco.
example.en: I finally managed to get some sleep.

cards.trick: CONSEGUIR sounds like "consequence": you managed to do it, and success is the consequence.

cards.hint: adjective, as in the only one

example.target: Eres la única persona que me entiende.
example.en: You're the only person who understands me.

cards.trick: ÚNICO sounds like "unicorn": the only unicorn in the world is the only one you'll ever see.
cards.why: Use único for "the only one" before or after a noun; use solo for "only" meaning just (solo quiero café).

example.en: Is this phone yours?

cards.trick: TUYO sounds like "to you": what belongs to you is yours.
cards.why: Use tuyo on its own or after the verb (es tuyo); use tu right before a noun (tu libro).

example.target: Mi vida cambió mucho este año.
example.en: My life changed a lot this year.

cards.trick: CAMBIAR starts like camera: change the camera lens and the whole picture changes.

cards.hint: a story or what happened, not decir

example.en: Tell me what happened last night.

cards.trick: CONTAR sounds like 'count tales': a storyteller counts out tales one by one as he tells them.
cards.why: Use contar to tell a story or what happened; use decir to say words or give a quick message.

cards.en: I'll call you [as soon as] I arrive

example.target: Te llamo en cuanto llegue a casa.
example.en: I'll call you as soon as I get home.

cards.trick: EN CUANTO sounds like in quantum: the moment, the quantum leap, as soon as it happens.

cards.hint: a story or topic, with de

example.en: What is the movie about?

cards.trick: TRATAR sounds like "tract": a tract is a booklet that's all about one topic.

example.en: Remind me to call my mom.

cards.trick: RECORDAR sounds like record: you play someone a recording to remind them.

example.en: Call the police right now!

cards.trick: POLICÍA sounds like police plus a cheer, AH: the police arrive and everyone says ah.
cards.why: Use la policía for the police force as a whole; el policía is one officer.

cards.hint: used instead of y before a word starting with an i sound (i-, hi-)

example.en: I speak Spanish and English.

cards.trick: E replaces Y before an EE sound, so you never say y-ee; padre e hijo flows smoothly.
cards.why: Use e instead of y only before a word starting with an i sound (i-, hi-): padre e hijo.

example.en: Wait for me a minute, I'm coming.

cards.trick: MINUTO sounds like minute-oh: oh, just one more minute!

cards.hint: neuter it after a preposition, a bit formal; not eso

example.target: Por ello no quiero hablar contigo.
example.en: That's why I don't want to talk to you.

cards.trick: ELLO sounds like hello: you say hello to it, the thing nobody names.

example.en: See you next week.

cards.trick: SEMANA sounds like 'seven-ana': Ana works seven days, one full week.

example.en: My family lives in Guadalajara.

cards.trick: FAMILIA sounds like "familiar": your family are the most familiar faces you know.

cards.hint: far from both speakers, not ese

example.en: That man over there is my uncle.

cards.trick: AQUEL sounds like "a kill": that hunter far away over there is about to make a kill.
cards.why: Use aquel for something far from both of you; ese for something near the person you're talking to.

example.target: Siempre estamos juntos en las fiestas.
example.en: We're always together at parties.

cards.trick: JUNTO sounds like "joined two": when two people are joined, they are together.

example.en: Anyone can do that.

cards.trick: CUALQUIERA sounds like "call-key-era": anyone who calls can get the key.
cards.why: Use cualquiera for anyone at all, whoever it is; use alguien for some particular person.

example.target: No te preocupes, todo va a estar bien.
example.en: Don't worry, everything's going to be fine.

cards.trick: PREOCUPAR sounds like pre-occupy: when you worry, your mind is preoccupied.

example.en: What do you know about her?

cards.trick: ACERCA sounds like a circle: you talk in circles about something.

example.en: Take out the trash, please.

cards.trick: SACAR sounds like sack-car: you take the sack out of the car.

example.target: No tengo dinero en mi cuenta.
example.en: I don't have money in my account.

cards.trick: CUENTA sounds like count-a: the bank counts every dollar in your account.

cards.hint: relative, after el/la/lo, no accent; not que

example.target: Llegó tarde, lo cual me molestó mucho.
example.en: He arrived late, which really bothered me.

cards.trick: CUAL sounds like the start of quality: the quality which matters most.

example.en: Are you ready to go out?

cards.trick: LISTO sounds like list: once you tick off every item on your list, you're ready.
cards.why: Use listo with estar for ready (estoy listo); with ser it means clever.

example.target: Ambos hermanos viven en la misma ciudad.
example.en: Both brothers live in the same city.

cards.trick: AMBOS sounds like "am both": I am both happy and tired, two things at once.

example.en: My uncle lives in Guadalajara.

cards.trick: TÍO sounds like "tea-oh": your uncle always shows up at teatime saying "oh, tea!"

example.en: Certain people don't know how to listen.

cards.trick: CIERTO looks like certain with the ending cut off: certain people, ciertas personas.

cards.hint: manner, as in the way to do it; not manera or modo, but the word that also means shape

example.target: No hay otra forma de hacerlo.
example.en: There's no other way to do it.

cards.trick: FORMA sounds like format: the format is the way you do something.

cards.hint: one word, also hers, theirs, yours (usted)

example.target: Ese carro no es mío, es suyo.
example.en: That car isn't mine, it's his.

cards.trick: SUYO sounds like "sue you": if you take what is his, he'll sue you.

example.en: You're right, I'm sorry.

cards.trick: If you have RAZÓN, you have the reason on your side, so you're right.

example.target: El viejo vive solo en esa casa.
example.en: The old man lives alone in that house.

cards.trick: EL VIEJO sounds like "the very yokel": the old man in overalls sitting on his porch.

cards.hint: the rest of the people, used after los; not otros

example.target: No te preocupes por los demás.
example.en: Don't worry about the others.

cards.trick: DEMÁS sounds like the mass: the whole mass of everyone else, the rest of them.

example.en: Are you crazy? It's really cold outside.

cards.trick: LOCO sounds like loco-motive: a crazy train speeding off the rails.

example.en: I slept very little last night.

cards.trick: DORMIR sounds like dorm: the dorm is where students go to sleep.

example.target: Gano poco dinero en este trabajo.
example.en: I earn little money at this job.

cards.trick: GANAR sounds like gain-ar: when you earn money at work, you gain cash.

cards.hint: but rather, correcting a negative (not pero)

example.target: No es mi hermano, sino mi primo.
example.en: He's not my brother, but my cousin.

cards.trick: SINO sounds like see, no: see, no, not that one, but rather this one.
cards.why: Use sino after a negative to give the right alternative (not X but Y); use pero to add a contrast.

cards.hint: situation or investigation, not a container

example.en: The detective solved the case.

cards.trick: CASO sounds like case-o: every detective's favorite word is case-o, the case to crack.

cards.hint: also yet in todavía no; not aún

example.en: Are you still at home?

cards.trick: TODAVÍA sounds like "today via": you're still on your way today, and you're not there yet.

example.en: Where are we going tonight?

cards.trick: ADÓNDE sounds like "a donde": add an A to dónde when you're heading toward somewhere.
cards.why: Use adónde to ask where someone is going (with motion); dónde for where something is.

example.en: My head really hurts.

cards.trick: CABEZA sounds like "cab bets ya": the cab driver bets you'll bump your head getting in.

example.en: Wait for me a second, I'm coming.

cards.trick: SEGUNDO sounds like "second, go!": the timer ticks one second and the race begins.

example.en: I'm on your side.

cards.trick: LADO sounds like "ladder": lean the ladder against the side of the house.

example.en: See you in the afternoon.

cards.trick: TARDE sounds like "tardy": the afternoon is the tardy part of the day, after the morning has gone.

example.target: Tras la cena, vimos una película.
example.en: After dinner, we watched a movie.

cards.trick: TRAS sounds like trace: you follow someone's trace, coming after and behind them.

example.en: This damn car won't start!

cards.trick: MALDITO sounds like bad ditto: bad, then bad again, so the thing must be cursed.

example.target: El policía le puso las esposas.
example.en: The police officer put the handcuffs on him.

cards.trick: ESPOSAS are like spouses: once they're on your wrists, you're bound together.

example.target: Salimos a pesar de la lluvia.
example.en: We went out despite the rain.

cards.trick: A PESAR DE: even with a problem weighing (pesar) on you, you keep going anyway.

cards.hint: excessively, as in too big; not also

example.en: This coffee is too hot.

cards.trick: DEMASIADO sounds like "the massive dough": that pizza dough is too big for the oven.
cards.why: Use demasiado for too meaning excessively (too hot); use también for too meaning also.

example.en: What does this word mean?

cards.trick: SIGNIFICAR sounds like "significant": anything significant means something.

example.target: Mi hija lee un libro cada semana.
example.en: My daughter reads a book every week.

cards.trick: LEER sounds like "leer": you leer at the page when you read the juicy gossip.

example.target: Abrimos todos los días salvo el domingo.
example.en: We're open every day except Sunday.

cards.trick: SALVO sounds like salvage: you salvage everything except the one piece that sank.

cards.hint: a game or sport, not music

example.target: Los niños juegan fútbol en el parque.
example.en: The kids play soccer in the park.

cards.trick: JUGAR sounds like "who guards" the goal? Whoever wants to play the game.
cards.why: Use jugar for games and sports; for playing music or an instrument, use tocar.

example.target: Tu abuela tiene un estilo único.
example.en: Your grandma has a unique style.

cards.trick: ÚNICO sounds like "unique-o": just say unique with an O on the end.

cards.hint: the everyday word, as in "it's a long story"; not a children's tale

example.en: It's a very long story.

cards.trick: HISTORIA sounds like his story: every person has his story to tell.

example.target: Vi a mi hermano a través de la ventana.
example.en: I saw my brother through the window.

cards.trick: TRAVÉS sounds like traverse: to traverse something is to go through or across it.
cards.why: Use a través de for through something to the other side, like a window; por for moving along or around a route.

example.target: Mi hijo ya cuenta hasta cien.
example.en: My son can already count to a hundred.

cards.trick: CONTAR sounds like 'counter': a counter is the thing that counts.

cards.hint: as in out of town, followed by de; the shorter word, not afuera

example.target: Mi papá está fuera de la ciudad.
example.en: My dad is out of town.

cards.trick: FUERA sounds like fury: in a fury, she threw him out of the house.
cards.why: Use fuera before de (fuera de la ciudad); afuera stands alone for outside.

cards.hint: two words, not pero or no obstante

example.target: Es caro. Sin embargo, lo voy a comprar.
example.en: It's expensive. However, I'm going to buy it.

cards.trick: SIN EMBARGO sounds like "seen an embargo": I've seen an embargo; however, the ships still sail.

example.en: Can you close the door, please?

cards.trick: PUERTA sounds like "portal": every portal starts with a door you walk through.

example.target: El policía me pidió mi licencia.
example.en: The police officer asked me for my license.

cards.trick: POLICÍA ends like see-ah: the officer says I see ya speeding, and writes you a ticket.
cards.why: Use el policía for one officer; la policía means the whole police force.

cards.hint: what you call a loved one, the same word that means affection (not amor, cielo, corazón or mi vida)

example.en: Honey, I'm home.

cards.trick: CARIÑO sounds like "carry no": honey, I'll carry you, no problem.

example.target: Mi hermano tiene un carro muy rápido.
example.en: My brother has a really fast car.

cards.trick: RÁPIDO sounds like rapid: rapids in a river are fast.

cards.hint: maintain, keep up; not store away

example.target: Mantén la calma, todo va a estar bien.
example.en: Keep calm, everything is going to be fine.

cards.trick: MANTENER sounds like "man, ten in here": a man keeps ten people in line by maintaining order.
cards.why: Use mantener to keep something going or in a state; guardar to put something away or store it.

example.target: ¡Qué genial! Vamos a la playa mañana.
example.en: How great! We're going to the beach tomorrow.

cards.trick: GENIAL sounds like genie: a genie granting your wishes would be great.

cards.hint: manner, how it is done; not camino, forma or modo

example.target: No hay otra manera de hacerlo.
example.en: There's no other way to do it.

cards.trick: MANERA sounds like manner: your manners are the way you do things.

cards.hint: the route you travel, not a manner

example.en: We're already on our way.

cards.trick: CAMINO sounds like came in, oh: you came in by this path, the only way through the woods.
cards.why: Use camino for the route you travel; manera or forma for the way something is done.

cards.hint: not pasar or ocurrir; looks like succeed

example.en: What's happening here?

cards.trick: SUCEDER sounds like succeed: when things succeed one after another, events happen.

cards.hint: two-word phrase, not claro, cómo no or desde luego

example.en: Will you help me? Of course.

cards.trick: POR SUPUESTO sounds like "for supposed": of course it's true, everyone supposed so.

example.en: You have really pretty eyes.

cards.trick: OJO sounds like "oh, ho!": your eyes go wide when you see something surprising.

example.target: Mi hermano es más bajo que yo.
example.en: My brother is shorter than me.

cards.trick: BAJO sounds like a baby's 'bah-ho': babies are short.

example.target: Te escribo un mensaje más tarde.
example.en: I'll write you a message later.

cards.trick: ESCRIBIR sounds like a scribe: an old scribe sits all day writing letters by hand.

cards.hint: to happen, a bit more formal than pasar

example.en: What happened last night at the party?

cards.trick: OCURRIR sounds like occur: things that occur are things that happen.

example.en: I fell in the street.

cards.trick: CAER sounds like "cry": you cry when you fall off your bike.

example.en: Your sister is very clever.

cards.trick: LISTO sounds like list: the clever kid knows the whole list by heart.
cards.why: Use listo with ser for clever (es muy listo); with estar it means ready.

cards.hint: before a noun, as in half an hour (not the noun mitad)

example.target: Te espero media hora, no más.
example.en: I'll wait for you half an hour, no more.

cards.trick: MEDIO sounds like medium: a medium portion is half of the big one.

example.en: Don't touch that, it's hot.

cards.trick: TOCAR sounds like "toe car": you touch your toe to the car to feel if it's hot.

example.en: Move, I can't see anything!

cards.trick: MOVER sounds like "mover": a mover is someone who moves things.

example.target: La nube tiene forma de corazón.
example.en: The cloud is shaped like a heart.

cards.trick: FORMA sounds like form: the form of something is its shape.

example.en: Can you open the door for me, please?

cards.trick: ABRIR sounds like abracadabra: say the magic word and every door opens.

example.target: Mi papá regresa del trabajo a las seis.
example.en: My dad comes back from work at six.

cards.trick: REGRESAR sounds like regress: to regress is to go back, so you come back where you started.
cards.why: Same meaning as volver; regresar is very common in Latin America, while Spain mostly says volver.

example.en: I'm sending you the photo now.

cards.trick: ENVIAR sounds like envoy: an envoy is someone you send with a message.

example.target: Me voy de viaje el próximo mes.
example.en: I'm going on a trip next month.

cards.trick: MES sounds like "mess": your room turns into a mess after a whole month without cleaning.

example.target: Mete la ropa en la maleta.
example.en: Put the clothes in the suitcase.

cards.trick: METER sounds like a parking meter: you put coins in the meter.
cards.why: Use meter for putting something inside something else; use poner for putting it somewhere, like on a table.

example.target: Mi jefe me llamó esta mañana.
example.en: My boss called me this morning.

cards.trick: JEFE sounds like "chef": the head chef is the boss of the kitchen.

cards.hint: the form used before de, not adentro

example.target: Las llaves están dentro de la caja.
example.en: The keys are inside the box.

cards.trick: DENTRO sounds like "den": you hide inside your den.

example.target: Casi me caigo en la calle.
example.en: I almost fell in the street.

cards.trick: CASI sounds like "classy": you're almost classy, but not quite.

cards.hint: of a machine or plan, not a job

example.en: My phone doesn't work.

cards.trick: FUNCIONAR sounds like "function": when something functions, it works.
cards.why: Use funcionar when a machine or plan works; trabajar when a person works at a job.

example.en: I want to have my own house.

cards.trick: PROPIO sounds like property: your property is your own.

example.en: See you soon, buddy.

cards.trick: PRONTO sounds like "pronto" in English: do it pronto means do it soon, right away.

example.target: No le tengo miedo a la muerte.
example.en: I'm not afraid of death.

cards.trick: MUERTE sounds like "more tea": at the wake, everyone asks for more tea after the death.

example.target: Te quiero con todo mi corazón.
example.en: I love you with all my heart.

cards.trick: CORAZÓN sounds like "core zone": your heart beats in the core zone of your chest.

example.en: You're really lucky.

cards.trick: SUERTE sounds like "sweat-a": you sweat a lot hoping for good luck.

cards.hint: also the title, as in Doctor García; not médico

example.en: I need to see the doctor today.

cards.trick: DOCTOR is spelled just like English; only the stress moves to the end: doc-TOR.

cards.hint: not perdonar or excusar; with -se it means to apologize

example.en: Excuse me, where is the bathroom?

cards.trick: DISCULPAR sounds like this culprit: please excuse this culprit, he didn't mean it.

example.target: Tienes razón, ese es un buen punto.
example.en: You're right, that's a good point.

cards.trick: PUNTO sounds like "punt": the kicker punts the ball to score a point.

example.target: Mi mamá prepara la cena todos los días.
example.en: My mom prepares dinner every day.

cards.trick: PREPARAR is just prepare with its final e swapped for -ar (prepar-AR), and you're ready to go.

example.target: Eso no es justo, yo llegué primero.
example.en: That's not fair, I got here first.

cards.trick: JUSTO sounds like justice: a fair judge always gives justice.

example.target: Tengo clase de inglés a las ocho.
example.en: I have English class at eight.

cards.trick: CLASE sounds like class: drop one S and add an E at the end of the lesson.

example.target: Mi perro duerme en el sofá.
example.en: My dog sleeps on the sofa.

cards.trick: PERRO sounds like a purring 'pair-oh': the dog growls 'grrr' with that rolling RR.

example.target: Lávate la cara antes de dormir.
example.en: Wash your face before you sleep.

cards.trick: CARA sounds like "car": you see your face reflected in the shiny car window.

example.en: That's the reality.

cards.trick: REALIDAD sounds like "real, dad": Dad tells you to face reality and keep it real.

example.en: Put the weapon down right now!

cards.trick: ARMA sounds like arm: you arm yourself with a weapon, and the army carries arms.

example.en: My brother is very tall.

cards.trick: ALTO sounds like altitude: things with high altitude are tall and high up.

example.target: Me encanta la historia de México.
example.en: I love Mexican history.

cards.trick: HISTORIA is just HISTORY with the Y swapped for an -IA ending, like many Spanish feminine nouns.

example.en: We're a good team, right?

cards.trick: EQUIPO sounds like 'a key pole': the whole team carries one key pole together to win.

example.target: No tenemos suficiente dinero para el viaje.
example.en: We don't have enough money for the trip.

cards.trick: SUFICIENTE sounds like 'sufficient': when you have a sufficient amount, you have enough.
cards.why: Use suficiente for just enough for a need; bastante leans toward plenty, a good amount.

example.en: Run, the bus is already coming!

cards.trick: CORRER sounds like courier: a courier runs through town delivering packages.

example.en: Will you show me your new room?

cards.trick: MOSTRAR sounds like most rare: you show everyone your most rare treasures.

example.target: El hecho es que no me llamaste.
example.en: The fact is that you didn't call me.

cards.trick: HECHO sounds like "echo": a fact keeps echoing back no matter how you deny it.

cards.hint: something you play, not a sports match

example.en: This game is really fun.

cards.trick: JUEGO sounds like "who - EGO": in every game, someone's ego wants to win.

example.target: Le tengo mucho cariño a mi abuela.
example.en: I have a lot of affection for my grandma.

cards.trick: CARIÑO sounds like "caring-o": affection is all about caring.

example.en: Stop the car, please!

cards.trick: PARAR sounds like 'parent': a parent always yells at you to stop.
cards.why: Use parar for everyday stopping; detener is more formal, for halting or arresting someone.

example.en: This exam is very difficult.

cards.trick: DIFÍCIL sounds like "difficult" with the ending cut off, because finishing the word was too hard.

cards.hint: short word shown at the end of a movie, not final

example.target: Me olvidé completamente de tu cumpleaños.
example.en: I completely forgot about your birthday.

cards.trick: COMPLETAMENTE sounds like "complete mentally": you finish the puzzle completely, even in your head.

example.target: Revisa tu teléfono, te mandé un mensaje.
example.en: Check your phone, I sent you a message.

cards.trick: REVISAR sounds like "revise": you check your work again before handing it in.

example.en: My dad built this house.

cards.trick: CONSTRUIR sounds like construct: to build is to construct something from the ground up.

example.target: Él no es tu enemigo, es tu hermano.
example.en: He's not your enemy, he's your brother.

cards.trick: ENEMIGO sounds like "enemy go": you yell "Enemy, go away!" at your rival.

example.en: I totally agree with you.

cards.trick: TOTALMENTE sounds like "total mental": you agree so totally, it's total mental agreement.

example.target: Vamos a nadar en el mar.
example.en: Let's go swim in the sea.

cards.trick: MAR sounds like marine: marines sail across the sea.

example.target: Vamos al centro a comprar ropa.
example.en: Let's go downtown to buy clothes.

cards.trick: CENTRO is the center of town, so going al centro means heading downtown.

cards.hint: adjective, as in a kind person

example.target: Eres muy amable, gracias por tu ayuda.
example.en: You're very kind, thanks for your help.

cards.trick: AMABLE sounds like amiable: a kind person is amiable and easy to love.

cards.hint: reflexive, used with de; not recordar

example.en: Do you remember me?

cards.trick: ACUERDO sounds like "a cord": tie a cord around your finger to remember.
cards.why: Use acordarse with me/te/se and de (me acuerdo de ti); recordar takes the thing directly (recuerdo tu nombre).

example.en: Don't shout at me, please!

cards.trick: GRITAR sounds like 'greet a car': you shout hello at every passing car.

example.target: Mi mamá está muy preocupada por ti.
example.en: My mom is very worried about you.

cards.trick: PREOCUPADO sounds like preoccupied: a worried mind is preoccupied with its problems.

cards.hint: very old, from long ago; not viejo

example.en: This church is very old.

cards.trick: ANTIGUO sounds like antique: antiques are ancient things from long ago.
cards.why: Use antiguo for things from long ago, like a historic church; use viejo for people or things that are simply old.

cards.hint: a natural talent, not a present

example.target: Tienes un don para la música.
example.en: You have a gift for music.

cards.trick: DON sounds like donate: nature donated a special gift to you at birth.

example.en: He didn't commit the crime.

cards.trick: COMETER sounds like comet: a rogue comet commits a crime by smashing into Earth.

cards.hint: the native Spanish word, not the borrowed souvenir

example.target: Te traje un recuerdo de México.
example.en: I brought you a souvenir from Mexico.

cards.trick: RECUERDO sounds like "record": a souvenir is a small object that records your trip.

example.en: My family always supports me.

cards.trick: APOYAR sounds like a pillar: a pillar is there to support you.

example.en: You ruined the surprise!

cards.trick: ARRUINAR sounds like "a ruin": when you ruin something, you leave behind a ruin.

example.target: Mi abuela sufre mucho por el frío.
example.en: My grandma suffers a lot from the cold.

cards.trick: SUFRIR sounds like suffer-ear: you suffer when someone screams in your ear.

example.target: Mi hermana estudia medicina en la universidad.
example.en: My sister studies medicine at the university.

cards.trick: UNIVERSIDAD sounds like university plus dad: Dad paid for your university.

example.target: La policía abrió una investigación sobre el robo.
example.en: The police opened an investigation into the robbery.

cards.trick: INVESTIGACIÓN looks almost like investigation: just swap -tion for -ción, like most -tion words.

cards.hint: an age, a number of years

example.target: Mañana mi hija cumple diez años.
example.en: Tomorrow my daughter turns ten.

cards.trick: CUMPLIR sounds like complete: on your birthday you complete another year.

example.en: It turns out he was right.

cards.trick: RESULTAR sounds like "result": how something turns out is its result.

example.target: Llego a las siete de la noche.
example.en: I'm arriving at seven at night.

cards.trick: SIETE sounds like "see a tea": you see a tea set with seven cups.

example.en: My head really hurts.

cards.trick: DOLER sounds like "dolor", the Spanish word for pain: anything that hurts gives you dolor.

example.en: He's a man of principles.

cards.trick: PRINCIPIO looks like principle: a good prince lives by his principles.

cards.hint: take up space, time or a place

example.en: This table takes up a lot of space.

cards.trick: OCUPAR sounds like 'occupy': the giant couch occupies the whole room.

example.target: Los niños están viendo tele en la sala.
example.en: The kids are watching TV in the living room.

cards.trick: SALA sounds like "saw a": I saw a sofa and TV, so I knew it was the living room.
